For the first time, the authors present a detailed account of the egg and larval biology of the Dogtooth tuna (Gymnosarda unicolor). The fertilised ovum, a spherical and transparent pelagic egg, was found to have a diameter of approximately 1.05 mm. Using the volume formula for a sphere, the calculated wet weight at birth, representing the mass of the newly hatched yolk-sac larva, is 0.0006 grams [Wwb = 0.0006 grams]. Following a short incubation period of only 3 days [ab = 3 days] at a stable water temperature of 26.5 °C [T = 26.5 °C], the chorion ruptured. The emerging prolarva, still reliant on its yolk reserves, initiates the lecithotrophic stage. This remarkably brief embryonic phase, coupled with the small size of the offspring, is characteristic of many tropical pelagic teleosts that rely on high fecundity and rapid development in warm surface waters to offset high larval mortality.

The juvenile and sub-adult growth phases are characterised by rapid somatic development and steady increases in body size. Sexual maturation, or puberty, is a critical life-history transition that occurs at a relatively modest size for this large-bodied predator. The total length at puberty, a key metric indicating the onset of reproductive capability, has been recorded at 71.3 centimeters [Lp = 71.3 centimeters]. At this length, somatic growth continues but is increasingly complemented by gonadal development. The corresponding wet weight at puberty, representing the body mass at which an individual reaches this milestone, is estimated at 5,000 grams [Wwp = 5,000 grams]. This relationship between length and mass at maturity is consistent with allometric growth patterns observed in other members of the Scombridae family, where a shift in energy allocation toward gamete production becomes evident soon after the attainment of this size threshold.

As individuals continue to grow beyond puberty, they eventually approach their asymptotic size. The ultimate total length, representing the maximum body length recorded for the species, reaches 248 centimeters [Li = 248 centimeters]. This apex predator attains a correspondingly substantial ultimate wet weight, with the largest documented adults achieving a body mass of 227,600 grams [Wwi = 227,600 grams]. Such a massive size, placing it among the larger members of the tuna and mackerel lineage, is supported by a powerful, streamlined body and a piscivorous diet that fuels rapid growth throughout its life. Reaching this enormous size is a slow process, however, and reflects a life-history strategy that invests heavily in somatic maintenance and predator avoidance before the inevitable onset of senescence and natural mortality.

Reproductive output in Gymnosarda unicolor is best understood by examining the spawning dynamics of large, reproductively active adults. A gravid female weighing approximately 69 kilograms, under the sustained thermal conditions of 26.5 °C [T = 26.5 °C] typical of its tropical habitat, demonstrates an impressive annual reproductive capacity. Field estimates based on relative fecundity of 315,244 eggs per kilogram of body mass indicate that a single female can achieve an annual output of approximately 20,000,000 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 20,000,000 eggs per year]. This strategy of a single, massive spawning pulse is common among tropical scombrids, allowing them to synchronize larval emergence with peak zooplankton abundance. The high fecundity is offset by the minute size of the newly hatched offspring, which weigh a mere 0.0006 grams [Wwb = 0.0006 grams], reflecting a classic brood-size versus offspring-size trade-off.

The maximum lifespan, or longevity, of the Dogtooth tuna has been a subject of considerable investigation, particularly given its importance for stock assessment and fisheries management. Under the stable thermal regime of 26.5 °C [T = 26.5 °C] that characterises its tropical habitat, the oldest documented individuals have an expected lifespan of 20 years [am = 20 years]. This lifespan, while lengthy for a fast-growing teleost, is notable when combined with its extremely large ultimate body mass. The delayed attainment of reproductive maturity, occurring only after reaching 5,000 grams [Wwp = 5,000 grams], suggests that this species employs a bet-hedging strategy. By living for two decades, a slow process, individuals maximise their reproductive opportunities, ensuring multiple spawning seasons and thereby buffering against the high inter-annual variability in larval survival that typifies the pelagic environment.
